title: How to extract and analyze pollen from internal organs and exoskeletons of fossil insects
protocol: Place the fossil specimen under the dissecting microscope.
Adjust the magnification and focus so the insect is clearly visible.
Make the drop small and place it in the middle of the slide.
Name the slide appropriately.
Attach nasal hair to a teasing needle with UHU glue.
Observe fossil fly with stomach/abdomen contents preserved using a stereomicroscope with normal incident light.
Observe fossil beetle with stomach/abdomen contents preserved using a stereomicroscope with normal incident light.
Remove thin chitin layer in gut/abdomen region of fossil fly to reveal hidden gut contents using a narrow teasing needle.
Turn on epi-fluorescence illumination to discover pollen adhering to the exoskeleton of a fossil insect.
Place a small drop of glycerine on a LM microscope slide and keep it close by.
Extract pollen from the exoskeleton of the fossil insect using a teasing needle or micromanipulator with nasal hair.
Dip the needle/micromanipulator into glycerine before touching pollen adhering to dry specimens to prevent electrostatic loss.
Loosen the pollen from the surface of the insect using a teasing needle.
Pick up the pollen grain with a micromanipulator (nasal hair).
Push the pollen grain along the surface with the micromanipulator until it adheres to the hair.
Dry most of the glycerine from the surface of an insect specimen quickly and carefully with a paper napkin, ensuring liquid is absorbed by the tissue without scraping the surface.
Extract the pollen using a teasing needle and/or micromanipulator (nasal hair).
Transfer the pollen into a glycerine drop on a LM microscope slide.
Dip the tip of the micromanipulator into the glycerine drop to detach the pollen automatically and leave it in the drop.
Place fossil insect specimen under dissecting microscope.
Check if the abdomen is flat or protruding.
Look for yellow or orange masses through the thin chitin membrane as an indicator of large amounts of pollen within the digestive system.
Place a small drop of glycerine on a LM microscope slide to keep close by.
Use a fine teasing needle to puncture the abdomen.
Scrape out part of the gut content.
Transfer the gut content into a glycerine drop on the LM microscope slide.
Produce acetolysis solution by mixing nine parts of 99% acetic anhydride with one part 95–97% sulfuric acid.
Wait until the fluid has cooled down.
Place a drop or two of acetolysis fluid on a new LM microscope slide.
Place the slide on a paper sheet under a fume hood.
Observe the fossil pollen grain in the glycerine drop on the old LM microscope slide using an erect image compound microscope equipped with a 10× or 20× objective lens.
Move the distal end of the micromanipulator (with nasal hair) between the LM microscope slide and the lens while observing the pollen grain through the eyepiece.
Dip the tip of the micromanipulator into the glycerine to pick up the pollen grain stored within the drop.
Brush or push the pollen grain towards the edge of the glycerine using the tip of the micromanipulator.
Push the pollen grain out of the glycerine until it adheres to the nasal hair and transfer it to the acetolysis liquid on a new LM microscope slide.
Dip the tip of the micromanipulator with the attached pollen into the acetolysis liquid for automatic detachment from the hair and remaining in the drop.

Light a tea candle and hold the LM microscope slide, with the pollen grain in the acetolysis drop, over the flame for 3–5 seconds to dissolve extra organic material on the surface of the pollen grain.
Place the LM microscope slide with the pollen grain in the acetolysis drop under the erect image compound microscope.
Extract the pollen grain from the acetolysis drop and transfer it back to the glycerine drop on the old LM microscope slide using the micromanipulator.
Observe the pollen grain in the glycerine drop with an erect image compound microscope equipped with a 10× or 20× objective lens having an approximately 10 mm working distance.
Use the micromanipulator to turn the pollen to an optimal position (polar and equatorial views) while observing it through the eyepiece of the LM.
Switch to a lens with higher magnification (50× or 60×).
Photograph the pollen grain at different foci (high-, low focus, optical section).
Position a stereomicroscope close beside an erect image compound microscope equipped with a 10× or 20× objective lens having an approximately 10 mm working distance.
Place an SEM specimen stub under the stereomicroscope using normal incident light.
Prepare ethanol in a small glass container along with a micromanipulator and a glass pipette with a narrow and pointed end for transporting ethanol.
Form a drop of ethanol on the surface of the SEM specimen stub with one hand.
Dip the tip of a nasal hair with the fossil pollen into the ethanol drop using the other hand.
Observe a clump of pollen from the abdomen of a fossil fly with SEM.
Place a single SEM specimen stub under the stereomicroscope.
Have a small container with fresh ethanol at your side.
Prepare a narrow pointed glass-pipette from 2 mm wide glass pipes.
Locate the pollen grain in the glycerine drop on the old LM microscope slide with an erect image compound microscope.
Move the distal end of the micromanipulator (with nasal hair) between the LM microscope slide and the lens.
Dip the tip of the micromanipulator into the glycerine.
Pick up the pollen grain stored within the glycerine drop using the micromanipulator.
Slowly move the pollen grain towards the stereomicroscope.
Dip the tip of the narrow pointed glass-pipette into the ethanol container.
Press the tip of the pipette on the surface of the SEM specimen stub to leave a tiny drop of ethanol.
Gently press the tip of the micromanipulator, with the attached pollen, into the drop of ethanol.
Add two to three additional ethanol drops to clean the glycerine thoroughly off the pollen grain.
Sputter coat the material placed on the SEM specimen stub with gold for 5 minutes to achieve a coating thickness of 20 nm.
Photograph the pollen using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) to capture overview and close-up images.
Place the SEM specimen stub under a stereomicroscope if needed.
Add a drop of ethanol to the sputtered sample so it engulfs the pollen grain.
Flip the pollen grain over using a micromanipulator before the ethanol evaporates.
Re-sputter the SEM specimen stub with the flipped pollen grain.
Photograph the flipped pollen grain again using the SEM.
Prepare the setup for TEM infiltration and embedding before transporting the pollen from the LM microscope slide or SEM specimen stub into glycerine.
Clean and dehydrate the pollen after transportation.
Embed and stain the pollen.
Cut the embedded pollen into sections.
Achieve satisfactory transmission electron microscopy (TEM) micrographs showing important ultrastructural features in different areas of the pollen wall.
Prepare the embedding solution (LV-Resin).
Mix the first two components in a clean, dust-free disposable lockable plastic beaker using a magnetic stirrer.
Add remaining ingredients to the mixture and mix well again.
Place a stereomicroscope, the embedding solution (LV-Resin), and a plastic pipette inside a fume hood.
Turn hood settings to lowest intensity to avoid losing pollen grains due to strong airflow.
Clean the embedding mold before use by adding pure acetone dropwise into the empty mold.
Use a pipette to reabsorb and dispose of liquids from the embedding mold.
Repeat cleaning steps until the embedding mold is clean.
Place the SEM specimen stub with the coated pollen under a stereomicroscope.
Dip the micromanipulator (with nasal hair) into glycerine and then use it to pick up the pollen grain from the SEM specimen stub.
Transfer the pollen grain into a drop of glycerine placed on a new LM microscope slide.
Study the pollen grain with the LM to ensure correct extraction.
Transfer the pollen grain directly from the SEM specimen stub into the embedding mold using the micromanipulator.
Strike the micromanipulator along the bottom of the embedding mold to transfer the pollen grain into the mold.
Add acetone dropwise into the embedding mold until it is half-full.
Add a few drops of fresh embedding media (1:2, acetone/LV-resin) into the embedding mold.
Use the micromanipulator to move the pollen grain towards the center of the embedding mold.
Trim a small section from a plastic pipette (1 mL pipette, 5 mm in diameter).
Place the trimmed plastic section over the pollen grain using forceps to restrain it in the center of the embedding mold.
Move the pollen grain towards the center of the embedding mold using the micromanipulator.
Let the sample stand for approximately 15 min at room temperature (20°C–22°C) until the acetone has evaporated.
Dropwise fill up the embedding mold with embedding media, ensuring not to overfill it.
Use the micromanipulator to move and manipulate suspended pollen grains inside the resin towards the center.
Polymerize the sample and block holders at 70°C for 6–12 hours.
Cut the specimen block out from the disposable embedding mold using a razor blade or scalpel.
Cut ultrathin sections at 70 nm with a cutting speed of 1 mm/s and slow return speed.
Pick up a section when contrasting structures appear for observation under LM.
Isolate a single section using micromanipulators (eyelashes).
Transfer the isolated section into a drop of water on a glass slide.
Place the slide on a hot plate at 70°C.
Stain the dry section with toluidine blue for a few seconds.
Wash the stained section with distilled water.
View the stained section under LM.
Continue cutting if pollen grain is reached in sections.
Cut fossil pollen grains as a whole or in series of ultrathin sections (70 nm).
Separate floating section-row(s) into smaller groups using two micromanipulators (eyelashes).
Stretch tissue sections using xylol vapors.
Transfer the stretched sections onto a formvar film-coated copper slot grid under a stereomicroscope.
Remove water from the loop using a pre-cut wedge-shaped filter paper.
Place grids into a grid-box with all grids oriented in the same direction.
Write a sectioning protocol including specimen details and grid-box number.
Store the box upside down or away from light to protect sections.
Treat ultra-thin sections on copper grids with 1% aqueous potassium permanganate solution.
Place small drop(s) of potassium permanganate solution on a piece of parafilm.
Use forceps to transfer the grid(s) from the box onto the staining drop(s) with section-side directed downwards.
Stain the sections for 5–7 minutes.
Make a row of 3–5 large drops of distilled water on a piece of parafilm for washing.
Transfer grids from the staining agent using forceps.
Wash each grid three times for 5 min in water drops.
Put the grids back into the grid box using forceps.
Soak excess water from the grids with a piece of filter paper.
Study the ultrastructure of the pollen wall with TEM.
Photograph interapertural areas of the pollen wall.
Photograph apertural areas of the pollen wall.
Note all pollen wall peculiarities.
